desc:
Build an array a of n positive integers (every element is at least 1) such that

  • neighbouring elements differ by at most 1: |a[i] - a[i+1]| ≤ 1, and
  • the sum of all elements is at most maxSum.

Among all such arrays make a[index] as large as possible and return that value.

Example: n = 4, index = 2, maxSum = 6 gives 2 (e.g. [1, 2, 2, 1] has sum 6; a value of 3 would need at least [1, 2, 3, 1], which sums to 7). For n = 6, index = 1, maxSum = 10 the answer is 3 ([2, 3, 2, 1, 1, 1] has sum 10).
hints: Instead of searching for the best array, ask: given a target value v for a[index], what is the smallest possible sum of the whole array?

To keep the sum small, let the values fall by exactly 1 per step on both sides of index until they reach 1, and stay at 1 afterwards. The needed sum can be computed with arithmetic-series formulas in O(1).

That minimal sum grows with v, so binary search the largest v in [1, maxSum] whose minimal sum is at most maxSum. For one side with len cells (the peak included) and peak v: if v ≥ len the sum is (v + v - len + 1) * len / 2, otherwise it is v * (v + 1) / 2 + (len - v).
editorial: For a fixed peak v, the cheapest array is a[i] = max(1, v - |i - index|): any cell closer to the peak than this would break the neighbour rule only if it were smaller, and every cell must be at least 1. Its sum is the left part (index + 1 cells ending at the peak) plus the right part (n - index cells starting at the peak) minus the peak, which was counted twice.

Each side is a descending staircase v, v-1, ..., that is cut off at 1. If the side has len cells and v ≥ len, it is the arithmetic series v, v-1, ..., v-len+1. If v < len, the staircase reaches 1 after v cells and the remaining len - v cells each contribute 1. The minimal total sum is increasing in v, so the largest feasible v can be found by binary search over [1, maxSum] in O(log maxSum) time with O(1) space. Use 64-bit arithmetic: the sums reach about 1018 during the search.
